spread.citation: Hall (2019), How many hours does it take to make a friend?, Journal of Social and Personal Relationships 36(4): 80 to 100 hours to become a friend, combined across both studies; roughly 50 hours to a casual friend and more than 200 to a close friend.

spread.reason: No study reports a half-life for closeness without contact; Roberts and Dunbar (2015) report that friendships decline faster than kinship.

tieMissingWeightPerHour.citation: Pull toward contacting a person for each hour of time together the tie has lost since the last contact. Tail span of one adjacent quartile interval is an authored assumption, not measured by JPMorgan Chase Institute, Cash Is King, September 2016, Figures 5–7; original PDF SHA256 e4ddf6731fd32b239ec9d0afd308791c3b0155fe9f8396b4d80a8221e268eef7.
openingEmployerCashBufferTailSpan.estimatedFrom: One openly unmeasured tail-span coefficient for a continuous piecewise-linear opening-state quantile curve. Uniform identity-keyed startup ranks, interpolation, endpoints and the generated-firm crosswalk remain unmeasured. Never chooses later actor decisions, refills cash or sizes stock to future survival.

spread.reason: Published q25/median/q75 anchors do not identify a coefficient interval, extrema, tail shape, full CDF or uniform identity rank interpretation. The real empirical IQR is retained separately on the thirteen ESTIMATED median rows and supplemental target; it is not this coefficient's uncertainty interval.

kinNearCountyShare.citation: Share of a resident's relatives who live in the household's county rather than elsewhere in the state; tuned so the share of adults whose nearest parent or adult child lives nearby, and whose every such relative does, fall between the PSID 2013 figures.

spread.citation: Choi, Schoeni, Wiemers, Hotz and Seltzer (2020), Spatial Distance Between Parents and Adult Children in the United States, Journal of Marriage and Family 82(2), PSID 2013: 74.8% of adults with a living parent or adult child have the nearest within 30 miles; 35.5% have all of them within 30 miles.

kinInterbirthYears.citation: Years between a mother's successive births in generated sibships and families; prototype choice pending an NSFG birth-interval source.

spread.reason: No empirical bound for this generation coefficient has been identified; it is checked through the kin and personality answer keys in the P15 receipt.

kinFirstBirthAgeSdYears.citation: Spread in years of a mother's age at first birth around the NCHS national mean for that year; prototype choice pending a natality spread source.

spread.reason: No empirical bound for this generation coefficient has been identified; it is checked through the kin and personality answer keys in the P15 receipt.

kinPaternalAgeGapYears.citation: Years by which a generated father is older than the mother; prototype choice pending an NSFG or natality paternal-age source.

spread.reason: No empirical bound for this generation coefficient has been identified; it is checked through the kin and personality answer keys in the P15 receipt.

kinMaleFertilityAgeShiftYears.citation: Years by which a man's children ever born by age lag the women's Census table; prototype choice pending an NSFG men's fertility source.

spread.reason: No empirical bound for this generation coefficient has been identified; it is checked through the kin and personality answer keys in the P15 receipt.

kinBirthdayLatestDayOfMonth.citation: Gregorian calendar: the shortest month has 28 days, so any month accepts a generated day from 1 to 28.

personalityHeritability.citation: Vukasovic and Bratko (2015), Heritability of personality: A meta-analysis of behavior genetic studies, Psychological Bulletin 141(4), 769-785: average heritability of personality about 0.40.

personalityUpbringingShift.citation: Standard-score shift per step of the canonical upbringing value added to a resident's temperament; prototype choice so upbringing still matters without overriding the sourced spread.

spread.reason: No empirical bound for this generation coefficient has been identified; it is checked through the kin and personality answer keys in the P15 receipt.

personalitySociabilityRiskCorrelation.citation: Costa and McCrae (1992), Revised NEO Personality Inventory (NEO-PI-R) and NEO Five-Factor Inventory Professional Manual, facet intercorrelations in the normative sample of 1,000 adults, as transcribed with permission in the psychTools R package dataset neo (version 2.6.4): E2 Gregariousness with E5 Excitement-Seeking, r = .34.
personalitySociabilityRiskCorrelation.estimatedFrom: The published facet correlation, applied to the latent temperament scores that the matching facets set (SG-P15-personality-mapping). The spread is the 95% interval for a correlation in a sample of 1,000 (Fisher transformation).

spread.citation: Fisher-transformed 95% interval for the Costa and McCrae (1992) value with N = 1,000.

personalityReliabilityImpulseCorrelation.citation: Costa and McCrae (1992), Revised NEO Personality Inventory (NEO-PI-R) and NEO Five-Factor Inventory Professional Manual, facet intercorrelations in the normative sample of 1,000 adults, as transcribed with permission in the psychTools R package dataset neo (version 2.6.4): C3 Dutifulness with C6 Deliberation, r = .45; deliberation is reversed to impulsiveness here, so the value is -.45.

spread.citation: Fisher-transformed 95% interval for the Costa and McCrae (1992) value with N = 1,000.

personalityReferenceAge.citation: Age whose facet curve value counts as average, so the age shifts center near the adult population; prototype choice.
